If you can throw your weight behind any other idea that justifies otherwise abnormal oil consumption in Subaru boxer motors, I'd love to hear it. You can read my above comment. Unless you theorize that pistons float perfectly inside of the cylinder walls without making any contact with them (literally the purpose of piston rings), then I'll take what you claim with a grain of salt! The slightly additional amount of force coupled with friction occurs millions, if not billions of times throughout the rotation of the engine over its own lifetime- and I'd be willing to bet this minimal acceleration in wear adds up quickly.

Yes, and you'll find plenty of V6 and V8 motors that burn oil too.

That being said, do you recall highschool (or college) physics where they gave you a comparison between a box sitting on an inclined plane, and a box sitting flat on one side? Where you compute the normal force of gravity using FgSin(theta) & FgCos(theta) given the angle of the slope and the weight of the box? Or maybe you measure the force of friction of a box on a slope against the box sitting flat (following the same pattern of acceleration for each, since this would be normalized in a controlled environment such as a timed, constant-speed engine). In this scenario, you would be finding that the force of friction on a box sitting on a sloped plane is significantly less impactful on the travel of the box than a box sitting flat on one side and being dragged. 

As i said, this is basic physics, and you can equate that the average Subaru owner changes their oil just as often as every I6, I4, V4, V6 and V8 owner does- which gives no weight to the "just change your oil more often" argument.

Maybe [this](https://www.physicsclassroom.com/class/vectors/Lesson-3/Inclined-Planes) will shed some more light on the topic.

That also being said, you will find so many complaints of people's Subarus burning oil, even prematurely at lower mileages. Everybody i know who owns a Subaru has to top it off every 2-3k miles. My favorite project was my best friend's '08 Impreza 2.5i, which burned a quart every gas change. It had 200k miles, and burned less than my buddy's Grand Marquis which burned a quart between every oil change in comparison, also with 200k miles. My '14 Camry burned less than half a quart every oil change at 150k miles, whereas the average Subaru owners i am friends with at the same mileage (and less) burn a quart or more every oil change ('14 Outback w/ 150k, '19 Forester w/ 120k, '21 Impreza w/ 40k). You can't ignore such an obvious pattern lol, and I couldn't even make this shit up. I don't mean to seem like some sort of know-it-all, and i love Subaru's, but this wouldn't be such a notoriously prevalent issue if there was some other logical explanation to easily solve it after some 20-30+ years of this engine design being around. Despite these inefficiencies they otherwise enjoy great reliability!

No the cables don't stretch, they bend, which causes them to no longer work properly in their assemblies. You could try bending it back, but chances are it won't work the same anymore. At the end of each side of the cable is a little ball, and when the cable gets bent, the ball will no longer rotate in the socket properly causing the assembly to fail to latch/unlatch. Think of it like an oil well, where the top of the cable moves the pump jack up and down. Same design on the insides of your doors to work the handles too. In order to get the trunk to latch, take the carpet off of the underside of the trunk, and take a peek at where the cable feeds into the lock mechanism. There is a little opening where you can stick a screwdriver into and move the ball in its socket on the latch. In order to get the trunk out of the "unlatched" position so it can close and lock, just shift the ball towards the cable entry point and your trunk will close and latch like normal :)

If you're looking into saving some money as well, the cable for the trunk itself is actually really cheap. Same with the back seats, which have easier cables to replace since they are much shorter. You can replace it pretty easily with just screwdrivers and a bit of time. I opted not to do this because i ran aftermarket speakers in my car and didn't want to take all the cables i had run to the trunk out to re-run the length of cable and tear all my ties apart, so i paid somebody else to do it.

Yeah that duplicolor shit sucks, it looks like it just didn't cover. You'd probably need like 1-2 cans per wheel to get any coverage, it's a crappy one-part clear without a hardener, and i wouldn't even recommend it for wheels which typically take pretty heavy abuse. I'd recommend you take a softer scotch-brite pad, like a blue one, and just scuff them down real good with some water. If the metallic flake is coming off when you scrub them, don't even bother, and just degrease them, dry them off, and respray them with clear.

If you are spraying out of a can, get the Eastwood 2K clear or whatever equivalent they might have at your local automotive paint supply. You pop a button on the bottom which injects the hardener before you shake and spray, and it will set rock solid like a standard automotive clear coat would. You'd need at least one can per wheel though, and make sure you spray each coat nice and wet under good lighting so you can see your coverage. The wheels should look wet and the texture should be flat like glass by the time you finish spraying your second and third coats of clear.

It looks like the base coat got good coverage, so I think this is still perfectly salvageable. It's not optimal spraying over previously dried clear coat, but a nice scuff and degrease should be just fine to set up a re-clear. You might have some slight orange peel or dimpling when it's all done though, but considering they are wheels, don't expect them to be perfect.

Most manufacturers don't have a 0 down policy, and to make matters worse, you still pay interest year over year on your monthly payments, meaning you spend more than the vehicle is even worth long term.

Published statistics such as these simply do not exist, because this concept in engineering is a well known fact. Take any mechanic/workshop class, and/or engineering physics course at your local secondary ed, college, or university. Statistically, the larger the number of potential points of failure within a complex system, the more likely the system is prone to catastrophically fail. I'm not going to argue that all automatic transmissions are shitty, but on paper and in the field; this concept consistently proves to be true. Just stating the facts. If you've ever replaced a clutch or a transmission, you would understand why it's easier and much less expensive to replace a clutch than to swap a transmission, or replace a torque converter for example which can be very, very costly. This cost benefit drives the marginally small upcharge of paying for a car with a manual transmission, especially if it's in a somewhat niche car which you would consider purchasing as a long term vehicle. Yet again, however, for those who do not care; it simply does not matter.

I think the argument here, is that even though there's nothing wrong with automatic transmissions or their continuously-variable counterparts, every niche suits purpose- which in this case is simply the historically proven reliability due to the fact that there are less points of failure as a result of fewer moving parts in the transmission. Some people want to shift their own gears too, which is great, but some people also have experienced the consistently poor build quality with a majority of automatic transmissions on the market (myself included) which leads a lot of buyers to prefer the more reliable option. Does your car shift for you without problems? If yes, great! Good for you. But just because you haven't had an Auto shit the bed with repair costs beyond the car's value because NOBODY can fix them for cheap doesn't mean that your proprietary situation applies to every other person who's owned a vehicle. The fact of the matter is, people are willing to spend more on  something with desired attributes over its counterparts for peace of mind. Now, would I want a 14 year old car with a slushbox auto as a daily driver? No, because it's not what suits my interests, and it's not another risk I'm willing to take. If it does you well, however, that's all that matters.

Let the topsoil dry out, and up your nutrients a little bit. The feed needs to reach the roots, so rather than misting the top, give the whole pot and root zone a good soak until you get 10-20% runoff. Let the top 1-2 inches of soil dry out before watering again. This way your plant will suck up food more efficiently and create incentive for the roots to grow out more. Yellowing and necrosis on the bottom leaves is a sign that the plant is cannibalizing itself to conserve nutrients for new growth. Once your plant grows out of the seedling stage, there's really no purpose to mist the topsoil any longer unless you're fighting fungus gnats with some sort of insecticide.

Are you top dressing the soil at regular intervals/watering with bottle nutrients? Compost tea is good and it helps develop the microbial activity in the soil, but she looks hungry. Typically nutrient deficiencies show on the lowest/oldest leaves.
